meta.title: English Grammar & Reading Test — B1 to C2 (for Indonesian Students)
meta.description: 40 mixed-type questions covering tenses, conditionals, relative clauses, passives, reported speech, reading comprehension, and error correction. Difficulty: B1–C2.
notes: The field 'difficulty' is added to each question for reference (CEFR level).
Some mcq and passage_mcq items have MORE THAN ONE correct answer. Read the question carefully.
For click_correct and multi_error, some clickable segments are correct — do not click them.

questions.question: My brother ___ coffee every morning before going to work.

name.id: Simple Present Tense — Orang Ketiga Tunggal

details_explanation.explanation: 'My brother' is a singular third-person subject, so the verb 'drink' takes -s and becomes 'drinks'.
details_explanation.introduction: The sentence describes a habit: drinking coffee every morning. The phrase 'every morning' signals the simple present tense. Because the subject 'My brother' equals 'he', the verb needs the third-person singular ending.

rules.title: 1. When to Use the Simple Present
rules.explanation: Use the simple present for habits, routines, and general facts. Time markers like 'every morning', 'every day', 'usually', and 'always' often appear.
rules.structure: Subject + simple-present verb (+ other information).
notes: 'Every morning' shows a repeated action, not an action happening right now.

rules.title: 2. Third-Person Singular Ending
rules.explanation: With he, she, it, or a singular noun, add -s or -es to the base verb in affirmative sentences.
rules.structure: He/She/It + verb-s/-es; I/You/We/They + base verb.
notes: Most verbs take -s: drink → drinks.
Verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -ss, -o take -es: watch → watches, go → goes.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: 'My brother' = 'he', so the correct form is 'drinks'. 'Drink' is the base form, 'is drink' is not grammatical, and 'drinking' needs a form of 'be' (is drinking).
rules.structure: My brother + drinks + coffee + every morning.
notes: Correct answer: B — drinks.

common_mistakes.wrong: My brother drink coffee every morning.
common_mistakes.correct: My brother drinks coffee every morning.
common_mistakes.reason: A singular third-person subject needs the -s form in the affirmative simple present.

common_mistakes.wrong: My brother is drink coffee every morning.
common_mistakes.correct: My brother drinks coffee every morning.
common_mistakes.reason: Do not put 'is' before a base verb. Use the simple present for a routine.

other_examples.sentence: My father drinks tea every evening.
other_examples.translation: Ayah saya minum teh setiap malam.

explanation.en: 'My father' is singular third person, so 'drink' becomes 'drinks'.
explanation.id: 'My father' adalah orang ketiga tunggal, sehingga 'drink' menjadi 'drinks'.

other_examples.sentence: They drink coffee every morning.
other_examples.translation: Mereka minum kopi setiap pagi.

explanation.en: 'They' is plural, so the base verb 'drink' is used.
explanation.id: 'They' adalah jamak, sehingga kata kerja dasar 'drink' digunakan.

other_examples.sentence: Siti goes to the office by motorcycle.
other_examples.translation: Siti pergi ke kantor naik sepeda motor.

other_examples.sentence: The students study English twice a week.
other_examples.translation: Para siswa belajar bahasa Inggris dua kali seminggu.

explanation.en: 'The students' is plural, so the base verb 'study' is correct.
explanation.id: 'The students' adalah jamak, sehingga kata kerja dasar 'study' benar.

questions.question: Rina has been learning English ___ she was in primary school.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Since' is used with a starting point in time (a clause or a point), and here the starting point is 'she was in primary school'.
details_explanation.introduction: The present perfect continuous describes an action that started in the past and continues now. We use 'since' + starting point and 'for' + length of time.

rules.title: 1. 'Since' vs 'For'
rules.explanation: 'Since' introduces the point when something started. 'For' introduces the duration.
rules.structure: since + starting point (2019, Monday, she was young) / for + period (three years, two months).
notes: Correct: since 2019, since last week, since she was a child.
Correct: for three years, for two hours.

rules.title: 2. Present Perfect Continuous Form
rules.explanation: Use have/has + been + verb-ing for actions continuing up to now.
rules.structure: Subject + have/has + been + V-ing.
notes: Rina has been learning English since 2018.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The clause after the gap is 'she was in primary school', which is a starting point, not a duration. Therefore 'since' is correct. 'For' would need a period like 'for ten years'.
rules.structure: Rina has been learning English + since + she was in primary school.
notes: Correct answer: B — since.
'During' and 'from' do not fit with the present perfect continuous in this structure.

common_mistakes.wrong: Rina has been learning English for she was in primary school.
common_mistakes.correct: Rina has been learning English since she was in primary school.
common_mistakes.reason: 'For' needs a length of time, not a clause describing a starting point.

common_mistakes.wrong: Rina is learning English since primary school.
common_mistakes.correct: Rina has been learning English since primary school.
common_mistakes.reason: An action continuing from the past to now needs the present perfect (continuous), not the present continuous.

other_examples.sentence: I have lived in Surabaya since 2015.
other_examples.translation: Saya telah tinggal di Surabaya sejak 2015.

explanation.en: '2015' is a starting point, so 'since' is used.

other_examples.sentence: We have waited for two hours.
other_examples.translation: Kami telah menunggu selama dua jam.

explanation.en: 'Two hours' is a duration, so 'for' is used.

other_examples.sentence: He has been working here since he graduated.
other_examples.translation: Dia telah bekerja di sini sejak lulus.

explanation.en: A clause describing the starting point follows 'since'.
explanation.id: Klausa yang menunjukkan titik awal mengikuti 'since'.

other_examples.sentence: They have known each other for ten years.
other_examples.translation: Mereka telah saling mengenal selama sepuluh tahun.

explanation.en: 'Ten years' is a period of time, so 'for' is correct.
explanation.id: 'Sepuluh tahun' adalah periode waktu, sehingga 'for' benar.

questions.question: I ___ in Bandung since 2015. (Choose ALL correct answers.)

name.en: Present Perfect vs Present Perfect Continuous
name.id: Present Perfect vs Present Perfect Continuous

details_explanation.explanation: With 'since 2015', both the present perfect ('have lived') and the present perfect continuous ('have been living') are correct because the situation started in the past and continues now.
details_explanation.introduction: Both forms are used for actions or states that began in the past and are still true. 'Since' marks the starting point, so a perfect form is required — not the simple past, simple present, or present continuous.

rules.title: 1. Present Perfect for States
rules.explanation: The present perfect (have/has + past participle) is used with state verbs and with situations that started in the past and continue.
rules.structure: I have lived in Bandung since 2015.
notes: 'Live' can be used in both the simple and continuous perfect forms.

rules.title: 2. Present Perfect Continuous for Ongoing Situations
rules.explanation: The present perfect continuous (have/has been + V-ing) emphasises the continuation of the action up to now.
rules.structure: I have been living in Bandung since 2015.
notes: Both sentences are grammatically correct and natural.

rules.title: 3. Why the Other Options Are Wrong
rules.explanation: 'Lived' (simple past) cannot be used with 'since' for a situation continuing now. 'Live' and 'am living' do not express the connection from the past to now.
rules.structure: Correct: have lived / have been living. Incorrect: lived / live / am living.
notes: Correct answers: A and B.

common_mistakes.wrong: I live in Bandung since 2015.
common_mistakes.correct: I have lived in Bandung since 2015.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Since' with a situation continuing to the present needs a perfect tense.

common_mistakes.wrong: I lived in Bandung since 2015.
common_mistakes.correct: I have lived in Bandung since 2015.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Lived' suggests the situation is finished; 'since 2015' means it continues.

other_examples.sentence: She has worked at that bank since 2019.
other_examples.translation: Dia telah bekerja di bank itu sejak 2019.

explanation.en: Present perfect with 'since' for a situation that continues.
explanation.id: Present perfect dengan 'since' untuk situasi yang berlanjut.

other_examples.sentence: She has been working at that bank since 2019.
other_examples.translation: Dia telah bekerja di bank itu sejak 2019.

explanation.en: Present perfect continuous is also correct here, with a focus on duration.
explanation.id: Present perfect continuous juga benar di sini, dengan penekanan pada durasi.

other_examples.sentence: We have known each other since we were children.
other_examples.translation: Kami telah saling mengenal sejak kami kecil.

explanation.en: 'Know' is a state verb, so the simple perfect form is used.
explanation.id: 'Know' adalah kata kerja keadaan, sehingga bentuk perfect sederhana yang digunakan.

other_examples.sentence: He has been studying Japanese for three years.
other_examples.translation: Dia telah belajar bahasa Jepang selama tiga tahun.

explanation.en: With a duration ('three years'), 'for' is used with the perfect continuous.
explanation.id: Dengan durasi ('tiga tahun'), 'for' digunakan bersama perfect continuous.

questions.question: The new library is ___ than the old one.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Modern' is a longer adjective, so the comparative is formed with 'more': 'more modern than'.
details_explanation.introduction: The word 'than' signals a comparison between two things, so we need the comparative form, not the superlative or the base form.

rules.title: 1. Short vs Long Adjectives
rules.explanation: Short adjectives take -er (taller, faster). Longer adjectives (two syllables or more, like 'modern', 'interesting', 'expensive') take 'more'.
rules.structure: more + long adjective + than
notes: Correct: more modern than.
Incorrect: moderner than.

rules.title: 2. Comparison Signal 'than'
rules.explanation: 'Than' is used only with comparatives. 'The most' belongs to superlatives, and 'as ... as' shows equality.
rules.structure: A is more modern than B. / A is the most modern. / A is as modern as B.
notes: 'Than' in the sentence requires a comparative.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Only 'more modern' fits the comparative structure with 'than'. 'Most modern' is superlative, 'moderner' is not a word, and 'as modern' needs 'as', not 'than'.
rules.structure: The new library is more modern than the old one.
notes: Correct answer: A — more modern.

common_mistakes.wrong: The new library is more moderner than the old one.
common_mistakes.correct: The new library is more modern than the old one.
common_mistakes.reason: Do not use 'more' and -er together.

common_mistakes.wrong: The new library is most modern than the old one.
common_mistakes.correct: The new library is more modern than the old one.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Most' is for superlatives; 'than' needs a comparative.

other_examples.sentence: This book is more interesting than that one.
other_examples.translation: Buku ini lebih menarik daripada buku itu.

explanation.en: A long adjective takes 'more' in the comparative.
explanation.id: Kata sifat panjang memakai 'more' dalam bentuk comparative.

other_examples.sentence: My bag is heavier than yours.
other_examples.translation: Tasku lebih berat daripada tasku.

explanation.en: A short adjective takes -er: heavy → heavier.
explanation.id: Kata sifat pendek memakai -er: heavy → heavier.

other_examples.sentence: This is the most expensive restaurant in town.
other_examples.translation: Ini restoran termahal di kota.

explanation.en: No comparison with 'than', so the superlative is used.
explanation.id: Tidak ada perbandingan dengan 'than', jadi bentuk superlatif digunakan.

other_examples.sentence: Her house is as big as mine.
other_examples.translation: Rumahnya sebesar rumahku.

questions.question: Had I known about the meeting, I ___ my presentation earlier.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Had I known' = 'If I had known' (third conditional). The result clause must be 'would have + past participle': 'would have finished'.
details_explanation.introduction: In formal English, the if-clause of the third conditional can drop 'if' and invert: 'Had I known...'. The result clause still uses 'would have + past participle'.

rules.title: 1. Third Conditional Structure
rules.explanation: The third conditional describes an unreal past situation and its imagined result.
rules.structure: If + had + past participle, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: If I had known, I would have finished earlier.

rules.title: 2. Inversion Instead of 'If'
rules.explanation: When 'if' is omitted, the auxiliary 'had' moves to the front of the clause.
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: Had I known = If I had known.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The result clause refers to an unreal past, so it needs 'would have finished'. 'Would finish' is second conditional, 'had finished' is past perfect, and 'will finish' is future.
rules.structure: Had I known about the meeting, I would have finished my presentation earlier.
notes: Correct answer: B — would have finished.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I known about the meeting, I would finish my presentation earlier.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known about the meeting, I would have finished my presentation earlier.
common_mistakes.reason: An unreal past result needs 'would have + past participle'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I knew about the meeting, I would have finished earlier.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known about the meeting, I would have finished earlier.
common_mistakes.reason: After inversion, use the past participle 'known', not the past form 'knew'.

other_examples.sentence: Had she left earlier, she would have caught the train.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya dia berangkat lebih awal, dia akan menangkap kereta itu.

explanation.en: Inverted third conditional with 'would have caught'.
explanation.id: Kondisional tipe ketiga terbalik dengan 'would have caught'.

other_examples.sentence: Had we taken a taxi, we would not have been late.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya kami naik taksi, kami tidak akan terlambat.

explanation.en: Negative result clause: would not have + past participle.
explanation.id: Klausa hasil negatif: would not have + past participle.

other_examples.sentence: If they had known the truth, they would have told us.
other_examples.translation: Jika mereka tahu kebenarannya, mereka akan memberi tahu kami.

other_examples.sentence: Had I studied harder, I would have passed the exam.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya saya belajar lebih giat, saya akan lulus ujian itu.

explanation.en: Both clauses show unreal past: 'had studied' + 'would have passed'.
explanation.id: Kedua klausa menunjukkan masa lalu tidak nyata: 'had studied' + 'would have passed'.

questions.question: Dewi said that she ___ that movie the night before.

details_explanation.explanation: After 'said that', the verb shifts one step back. 'Saw' (simple past) becomes 'had seen' (past perfect).
details_explanation.introduction: When the reporting verb is in the past ('said'), the reported verb usually moves one tense back. The time expression 'the night before' also shows that the earlier action happened before the reporting.

rules.title: 1. Backshift Rule
rules.explanation: Present → past, past → past perfect, will → would.
rules.structure: Direct: 'I saw it.' → Reported: She said she had seen it.
notes: Simple past becomes past perfect.

rules.title: 2. Time Expressions Change Too
rules.explanation: 'Last night' becomes 'the night before', 'now' becomes 'then', 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.
rules.structure: last night → the night before
notes: The phrase 'the night before' in the sentence confirms a past-perfect context.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The original would be 'I saw that movie last night.' Reported with a past reporting verb, it becomes 'she had seen that movie the night before'.
rules.structure: Dewi said that she had seen that movie the night before.
notes: Correct answer: B — had seen.

common_mistakes.wrong: Dewi said that she has seen that movie the night before.
common_mistakes.correct: Dewi said that she had seen that movie the night before.
common_mistakes.reason: The reported verb must shift back when the reporting verb is past.

common_mistakes.wrong: Dewi said that she seen that movie the night before.
common_mistakes.correct: Dewi said that she had seen that movie the night before.
common_mistakes.reason: The past perfect needs the auxiliary 'had'.

other_examples.sentence: He said he was tired.
other_examples.translation: Dia berkata bahwa dia lelah.

other_examples.sentence: She told me she would call me the next day.
other_examples.translation: Dia memberitahuku bahwa dia akan meneleponku keesokan harinya.

other_examples.sentence: They said they had finished the project the week before.
other_examples.translation: Mereka berkata bahwa mereka telah menyelesaikan proyek itu minggu sebelumnya.

explanation.en: Past simple shifts back to past perfect.
explanation.id: Simple past berubah menjadi past perfect.

other_examples.sentence: My teacher said that water boils at 100 degrees.
other_examples.translation: Guru saya berkata bahwa air mendidih pada 100 derajat.

explanation.en: General truths do not need backshift.
explanation.id: Kebenaran umum tidak perlu pergeseran tenses.

questions.question: The woman ___ lives next door is a doctor. (Choose ALL correct answers.)

name.id: Kata Ganti Relatif — Klausa Relatif Penentu

details_explanation.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of 'lives', and the antecedent is a person ('the woman'). Both 'who' and 'that' are correct.
details_explanation.introduction: In a defining relative clause about a person, we use 'who' or 'that' as the subject. 'Which' is for things, 'whom' is for objects, and 'whose' shows possession.

rules.title: 1. Subject Relative Pronouns
rules.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' for people when the relative pronoun is the subject of the clause.
rules.structure: The woman who/that lives next door...
notes: Do not use 'whom' as a subject.

rules.title: 2. Which / Whose / Whom
rules.explanation: 'Which' refers to things or animals. 'Whose' means 'of whom'. 'Whom' is used as an object, not as a subject.
rules.structure: The book which/that is on the table... / The man whose car was stolen...
notes: 'Whom' cannot be followed by a verb like 'lives'.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Since 'the woman' is a person and the relative pronoun is the subject of 'lives', both 'who' and 'that' are grammatically correct.
rules.structure: The woman who/that lives next door is a doctor.
notes: Correct answers: A and C.

common_mistakes.wrong: The woman which lives next door is a doctor.
common_mistakes.correct: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Which' cannot refer to a person.

common_mistakes.wrong: The woman whom lives next door is a doctor.
common_mistakes.correct: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Whom' is an object pronoun and cannot be the subject of 'lives'.

other_examples.sentence: The man who/that teaches us is very patient.
other_examples.translation: Pria yang mengajar kami sangat sabar.

explanation.en: Both 'who' and 'that' work as subject pronouns for people.
explanation.id: Baik 'who' maupun 'that' berfungsi sebagai subjek untuk orang.

other_examples.sentence: The laptop which/that I bought is very fast.
other_examples.translation: Laptop yang saya beli sangat cepat.

other_examples.sentence: The student whose essay won the prize is my cousin.
other_examples.translation: Siswa yang esainya memenangkan hadiah adalah sepupuku.

other_examples.sentence: The teacher whom we met yesterday is from Bandung.
other_examples.translation: Guru yang kami temui kemarin berasal dari Bandung.

questions.question: She has ___ finished her homework, so she can go out now. (Choose ALL correct answers.)

details_explanation.explanation: In an affirmative present perfect sentence, 'already' and 'just' both fit: 'has already finished' and 'has just finished'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Already' shows something happened earlier than expected. 'Just' shows it happened a very short time ago. 'Yet' is used in negatives and questions, 'ever' in questions about experience, and 'since' needs a starting point.

rules.title: 1. Position of 'already' and 'just'
rules.explanation: Both go between the auxiliary 'has/have' and the past participle.
rules.structure: Subject + have/has + already/just + past participle.
notes: She has already finished. / She has just finished.

rules.title: 2. 'Yet', 'ever', 'since'
rules.explanation: 'Yet' is used in negatives and questions. 'Ever' is used mainly in questions. 'Since' introduces a starting point, not a completed action.
rules.structure: Have you finished yet? / Have you ever been to Bali? / since 2019
notes: 'She has yet finished' is incorrect in standard English.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The sentence is affirmative and describes a completed action with a present result, so both 'already' and 'just' are correct.
rules.structure: She has already/just finished her homework.
notes: Correct answers: A and C.

common_mistakes.wrong: She has finished her homework yet.
common_mistakes.correct: She has already finished her homework.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Yet' is normally used in negatives and questions.

common_mistakes.wrong: She has ever finished her homework.
common_mistakes.correct: She has already finished her homework.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Ever' is used mainly in questions about experience.

other_examples.sentence: I have already eaten, thank you.
other_examples.translation: Saya sudah makan, terima kasih.

explanation.en: 'Already' shows the action happened earlier than expected.
explanation.id: 'Already' menunjukkan tindakan terjadi lebih awal dari yang diperkirakan.

other_examples.sentence: They have just arrived at the airport.
other_examples.translation: Mereka baru saja tiba di bandara.

explanation.id: 'Just' menunjukkan tindakan yang baru saja terjadi.

other_examples.sentence: Have you finished your report yet?
other_examples.translation: Apakah kamu sudah menyelesaikan laporanmu?

other_examples.sentence: She hasn't called me yet.
other_examples.translation: Dia belum menelepon saya.

questions.question: Which words can complete this polite request for permission? (Choose ALL correct answers.) ___ I use your phone for a moment, please?

name.id: Kata Kerja Modal untuk Meminta Izin

details_explanation.explanation: 'May', 'Can', and 'Could' can all be used to ask for permission. 'May' and 'Could' are more formal and polite; 'Can' is common in everyday speech.
details_explanation.introduction: To ask for permission in English we commonly use May I...?, Can I...?, and Could I...? 'Must' asks about obligation and 'Need' asks about necessity, so they do not express a polite request for permission.

rules.title: 1. Permission Modals
rules.explanation: Use may/can/could + base verb to ask for permission.
rules.structure: May/Can/Could + I + base verb?
notes: May I use your phone? (formal)
Could I use your phone? (polite)
Can I use your phone? (neutral, everyday)

rules.title: 2. Obligation and Necessity Modals
rules.explanation: 'Must' expresses strong obligation or a logical conclusion. 'Need' asks about necessity. Neither is used to ask politely for permission.
rules.structure: Must I...? / Need I...?
notes: 'Must I use your phone?' would ask whether there is an obligation to use the phone, which is not a permission request.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The sentence is a polite request with 'please', so A, B, and C all fit correctly.
rules.structure: May/Can/Could I use your phone for a moment, please?
notes: Correct answers: A, B, and C.

common_mistakes.wrong: Must I use your phone, please?
common_mistakes.correct: May I use your phone, please?
common_mistakes.reason: 'Must' asks about obligation, not permission.

common_mistakes.wrong: May I to use your phone?
common_mistakes.correct: May I use your phone?
common_mistakes.reason: Modals are followed by the base verb without 'to'.

other_examples.sentence: May I come in?
other_examples.translation: Bolehkah saya masuk?

explanation.en: A formal way to ask for permission.

other_examples.sentence: Can I borrow your pen?
other_examples.translation: Bolehkah saya meminjam pulpenmu?

explanation.en: An everyday, neutral way to ask for permission.
explanation.id: Cara sehari-hari yang netral untuk meminta izin.

other_examples.sentence: Could I ask you a question, please?
other_examples.translation: Bolehkah saya bertanya sesuatu?

other_examples.sentence: You must wear a helmet here.
other_examples.translation: Kamu wajib memakai helm di sini.

questions.question: The suspect denied ___ the money from the safe. (Choose ALL correct answers.)

details_explanation.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund: 'denied taking' or, for an earlier action, 'denied having taken'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some verbs are followed only by a gerund (-ing form). 'Deny' is one of them. The perfect gerund 'having + past participle' is used when the action clearly happened before the denying.

rules.title: 1. Verbs Followed by Gerunds
rules.explanation: Verbs such as deny, admit, suggest, enjoy, avoid, and mind take a gerund, not an infinitive.
rules.structure: deny + V-ing
notes: He denied stealing the money.
He suggested going by taxi.

rules.title: 2. Perfect Gerund for Earlier Actions
rules.explanation: When the gerund action happened before the main verb, use 'having + past participle'.
rules.structure: deny + having + past participle
notes: She denied having seen the letter.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Both 'taking' and 'having taken' are correct after 'denied'. 'To take', 'take', and 'took' do not fit the verb pattern of 'deny'.
rules.structure: The suspect denied taking/having taken the money from the safe.
notes: Correct answers: B and C.

common_mistakes.wrong: The suspect denied to take the money.
common_mistakes.correct: The suspect denied taking the money.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive.

common_mistakes.wrong: The suspect denied take the money.
common_mistakes.correct: The suspect denied taking the money.
common_mistakes.reason: A base verb cannot follow 'deny' directly.

other_examples.sentence: He admitted breaking the window.
other_examples.translation: Dia mengakui telah memecahkan jendela.

other_examples.sentence: She denied having met him before.
other_examples.translation: Dia membantah pernah bertemu dengannya sebelumnya.

explanation.en: The perfect gerund shows an earlier action.
explanation.id: Perfect gerund menunjukkan tindakan yang lebih awal.

other_examples.sentence: They suggested postponing the meeting.
other_examples.translation: Mereka menyarankan menunda pertemuan.

other_examples.sentence: I enjoy reading Indonesian novels.
other_examples.translation: Saya menikmati membaca novel Indonesia.

questions.question: The new bridge ___ next year.

details_explanation.explanation: The bridge receives the action, so a passive form is needed: 'will be + past participle' → 'will be built'.
details_explanation.introduction: In the passive voice, the object of the action becomes the subject. The future passive is formed with 'will be' + past participle.

rules.title: 1. Active vs Passive
rules.explanation: Active: The government will build the bridge. Passive: The bridge will be built (by the government).
rules.structure: Object + will be + past participle (+ by + agent).
notes: The agent is often omitted when it is unknown or unimportant.

rules.title: 2. Passive Forms by Tense
rules.explanation: The passive changes with the tense of 'be'.
rules.structure: is built (present) / was built (past) / will be built (future) / has been built (present perfect).
notes: 'Will been built' is never correct; 'been' needs 'have/has/had'.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The bridge cannot build itself, so 'will build' and 'is building' are wrong. 'Will been built' is ungrammatical. Only 'will be built' is correct.
rules.structure: The new bridge will be built next year.
notes: Correct answer: A — will be built.

common_mistakes.correct: The new bridge will be built next year.
common_mistakes.reason: The subject receives the action, so the passive is required.

common_mistakes.correct: The new bridge will be built next year.
common_mistakes.reason: Use 'be' after 'will', not 'been'.

questions.question: She is ___ honest person who always keeps her promises.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (/ɒ/), so 'an' is used: 'an honest person'.
details_explanation.introduction: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the SOUND of the next word, not the spelling. 'Honest' starts with a silent 'h', so the first sound is a vowel.

rules.title: 1. A vs An
rules.explanation: Use 'a' before consonant sounds and 'an' before vowel sounds.
rules.structure: a + consonant sound / an + vowel sound
notes: a university (yoo sound), a European country
an honest man, an hour, an MBA

rules.title: 2. Indefinite Article with Singular Countable Nouns
rules.explanation: We use a/an when introducing a singular countable noun that is not specific.
rules.structure: She is a teacher. He is an engineer.
notes: 'Person' is singular and countable, so an article is needed.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: 'Honest' has a silent h and starts with a vowel sound, so 'an' is correct. 'The' would suggest a specific person already known, and no article is not possible with a singular countable noun.
rules.structure: She is an honest person.
notes: Correct answer: B — an.

common_mistakes.wrong: She is a honest person.
common_mistakes.correct: She is an honest person.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the 'h' is silent.

common_mistakes.wrong: She is honest person.
common_mistakes.correct: She is an honest person.
common_mistakes.reason: A singular countable noun needs an article.

questions.question: I wish I ___ more attention in class yesterday.

details_explanation.explanation: A regret about the past is expressed with 'wish + had + past participle': 'I wish I had paid more attention'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Wish' changes meaning depending on the tense that follows. Past simple = present regret, past perfect = past regret, 'would' = wish for a change in someone's behaviour.

rules.title: 1. Wish + Past Simple
rules.explanation: Used for an unreal present situation.
rules.structure: I wish I had more money. (= but I don't)
notes: Refers to the present, not the past.

rules.title: 2. Wish + Past Perfect
rules.explanation: Used for regrets about the past.
rules.structure: I wish I had studied harder.
notes: The time marker 'yesterday' in this question shows the regret is about the past.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Because 'yesterday' is in the past, 'had paid' is needed. 'Paid' would refer to the present, 'would pay' does not fit 'I wish I...', and 'pay' is the base form.
rules.structure: I wish I had paid more attention in class yesterday.
notes: Correct answer: B — had paid.

common_mistakes.wrong: I wish I paid more attention in class yesterday.
common_mistakes.correct: I wish I had paid more attention in class yesterday.
common_mistakes.reason: A past regret needs the past perfect after 'wish'.

common_mistakes.wrong: I wish I would have paid more attention.
common_mistakes.correct: I wish I had paid more attention.
common_mistakes.reason: Do not use 'would have' after 'I wish I...' for a personal regret.

questions.question: Are you interested ___ joining our study group?

details_explanation.explanation: The adjective 'interested' is always followed by the preposition 'in': 'interested in + noun/V-ing'.
details_explanation.introduction: Many adjectives are followed by a fixed preposition. These collocations must be memorised: interested in, good at, afraid of, proud of, worried about.

rules.title: 1. Common Adjective + Preposition Pairs
rules.explanation: Learn the pairs as fixed units.
rules.structure: interested in / good at / afraid of / proud of / worried about / famous for
notes: Interested in music, interested in learning English.

rules.title: 2. Preposition + Gerund
rules.explanation: When a verb follows a preposition, it takes the -ing form.
rules.structure: interested in + V-ing
notes: Interested in joining (not 'to join').

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Only 'in' combines with 'interested'. 'On', 'at', and 'about' do not form this collocation.
rules.structure: Are you interested in joining our study group?
notes: Correct answer: B — in.

common_mistakes.correct: Are you interested in joining our study group?
common_mistakes.reason: 'Interested' is followed by 'in', not 'on'.

common_mistakes.correct: Are you interested in joining our study group?
common_mistakes.reason: A verb after a preposition must be in the -ing form.

questions.question: Not until she arrived home ___ that she had left her keys at the office.

details_explanation.explanation: When a sentence begins with a negative adverbial such as 'Not until...', the main clause takes question-word order: 'did she realize'.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative or restrictive adverbials placed at the beginning of a sentence trigger inversion of the subject and auxiliary in the main clause.

rules.title: 1. Negative Adverbials that Trigger Inversion
rules.explanation: Not until, never, seldom, rarely, hardly, no sooner, and not only cause inversion when they start the sentence.
rules.structure: Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb
notes: Never have I seen such a sight.
No sooner had he arrived than it started to rain.

rules.title: 2. Inversion with the Simple Past
rules.explanation: If there is no auxiliary, use do/does/did + subject + base verb.
rules.structure: Not until she arrived home did she realize...
notes: 'Did' carries the past tense; the main verb stays in the base form.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The sentence starts with 'Not until', so the main clause must invert: 'did she realize'. The other options use normal word order and are incorrect after this opening.
rules.structure: Not until she arrived home did she realize that she had left her keys at the office.
notes: Correct answer: B — did she realize.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not until she arrived home she realized that she had left her keys.
common_mistakes.correct: Not until she arrived home did she realize that she had left her keys.
common_mistakes.reason: The fronted negative adverbial requires inversion.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not until she arrived home she did realized.
common_mistakes.correct: Not until she arrived home did she realize.
common_mistakes.reason: After 'did', use the base verb 'realize'.

questions.question: If I ___ you, I would apologize to her immediately.

name.id: Kondisional Tipe Kedua — 'If I were you'

details_explanation.explanation: The second conditional uses 'if + past simple' and 'would + base verb'. With 'be', the fixed expression is 'If I were you'.
details_explanation.introduction: The second conditional describes an unreal or hypothetical present situation. 'If I were you' is a fixed formula used to give advice.

rules.title: 1. Second Conditional Structure
rules.explanation: Use past simple in the if-clause and 'would + base verb' in the result clause.
rules.structure: If + past simple, subject + would + base verb.
notes: If I had more money, I would travel.

rules.title: 2. 'Were' with All Subjects
rules.explanation: In the second conditional, 'were' is used with all subjects, especially in the fixed phrase 'If I were you'.
rules.structure: If I/he/she/it were...
notes: 'If I were you' is the standard advice formula.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The result clause 'would apologize' shows a second conditional, so the if-clause needs 'were'. 'Am', 'had been', and 'will be' do not fit this pattern.
rules.structure: If I were you, I would apologize to her immediately.
notes: Correct answer: B — were.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I am you, I would apologize.
common_mistakes.correct: If I were you, I would apologize.
common_mistakes.reason: The second conditional uses the past form 'were', not the present 'am'.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I were you, I will apologize.
common_mistakes.correct: If I were you, I would apologize.
common_mistakes.reason: The result clause of the second conditional uses 'would'.

questions.question: It was ___ a difficult exam that most students failed it.

details_explanation.explanation: Before 'a + adjective + noun', use 'such': 'such a difficult exam'. 'So' is used before an adjective without a noun: 'so difficult'.
details_explanation.introduction: Both 'so' and 'such' can introduce a result clause with 'that', but their grammatical patterns are different.

rules.title: 1. 'so' + adjective/adverb
rules.explanation: 'So' is followed directly by an adjective or adverb.
rules.structure: so + adjective + that ...
notes: The exam was so difficult that most students failed it.

rules.title: 2. 'such' + (a/an) + adjective + noun
rules.explanation: 'Such' is followed by a noun phrase.
rules.structure: such + a/an + adjective + singular noun + that ... / such + adjective + plural noun + that ...
notes: It was such a difficult exam that...
They were such difficult questions that...

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The phrase after the gap is 'a difficult exam', a noun phrase, so 'such' is needed. 'So' would require 'so difficult an exam' or 'the exam was so difficult'. 'Too' and 'very' do not fit the 'that' result structure here.
rules.structure: It was such a difficult exam that most students failed it.
notes: Correct answer: B — such.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was so a difficult exam that most students failed it.
common_mistakes.correct: It was such a difficult exam that most students failed it.
common_mistakes.reason: 'So' cannot be followed by 'a + adjective + noun'.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was such difficult exam that most students failed it.
common_mistakes.correct: It was such a difficult exam that most students failed it.
common_mistakes.reason: A singular countable noun needs 'a' after 'such'.

questions.question: You have finished your assignment, ___?

name.en: Question Tags with the Present Perfect

details_explanation.explanation: The statement is affirmative and uses 'have', so the tag must be negative and use the same auxiliary: 'haven't you'.
details_explanation.introduction: A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the main clause and reverses the polarity: positive statement → negative tag.

rules.title: 1. Polarity Rule
rules.explanation: Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag.
rules.structure: You have finished, haven't you? / You haven't finished, have you?
notes: The subject in the tag is always a pronoun.

rules.title: 2. Repeating the Auxiliary
rules.explanation: Use the same auxiliary as the main clause. In the present perfect, that is have/has.
rules.structure: have/has + pronoun (+ not)
notes: 'Don't you' would require a present simple statement.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The statement 'You have finished your assignment' is positive and uses 'have', so the correct tag is 'haven't you'.
rules.structure: You have finished your assignment, haven't you?
notes: Correct answer: A — haven't you.

common_mistakes.wrong: You have finished your assignment, have you?
common_mistakes.correct: You have finished your assignment, haven't you?
common_mistakes.reason: A positive statement takes a negative tag.

common_mistakes.correct: You have finished your assignment, haven't you?
common_mistakes.reason: The tag must repeat the auxiliary 'have'.

questions.passage: Siti is a student from Surabaya. She studies at a vocational school. Every day, she takes the bus to school at 6:30 a.m. Her classes begin at 7:15 a.m. and finish at 2 p.m. After school, she helps her mother in their small shop.
questions.question: What time do Siti's classes begin?

details_explanation.explanation: The passage states: 'Her classes begin at 7:15 a.m.' Therefore the answer is B.
details_explanation.introduction: A detail question asks for a specific piece of information stated directly in the text. Scan the passage for the keywords in the question: 'classes' and 'begin'.

rules.title: 1. Find the Keywords
rules.explanation: Look for the exact words or synonyms from the question in the passage.
rules.structure: Question: classes begin → Passage: Her classes begin at 7:15 a.m.
notes: The answer is stated directly; no inference is needed.

rules.title: 2. Distinguish Similar Details
rules.explanation: The passage contains several times. Match each time to the correct action.
rules.structure: 6:30 a.m. = takes the bus; 7:15 a.m. = classes begin; 2 p.m. = classes finish.
notes: Option A (6:30 a.m.) is when she takes the bus, not when classes start.

rules.title: 3. Match the Detail to the Options
rules.explanation: 'Her classes begin at 7:15 a.m.' matches option B exactly.
rules.structure: 7:15 a.m. → Option B.
notes: Correct answer: B — 7:15 a.m.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing 6:30 a.m. because it is the first time mentioned.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose 7:15 a.m. because the question asks when classes begin.
common_mistakes.reason: 6:30 a.m. is when Siti takes the bus.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing 2 p.m. because it is also in the passage.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose 7:15 a.m., the stated start time.
common_mistakes.reason: 2 p.m. is when her classes finish.

questions.passage: Budi had saved money for months to buy a new bicycle. However, when he heard that his friend's house had been damaged by a flood, he gave the money to help his friend's family. He now walks to school, but he says he has never regretted his decision.
questions.question: What can we infer about Budi?

options.B: He regrets giving his money away.
options.C: He values helping others more than buying things for himself.
options.D: He no longer goes to school.

details_explanation.explanation: Budi gave up his savings to help a friend and never regretted it. This shows he values helping others more than buying something for himself.
details_explanation.introduction: An inference question asks you to draw a conclusion that is supported by the text but not stated directly.

rules.title: 1. Inference vs Detail
rules.explanation: A detail is stated word for word; an inference must be logically supported by several details.
rules.structure: Detail: he gave the money. Inference: he values helping others.
notes: The correct inference must be supported by the whole passage.

rules.title: 2. Eliminate Options Contradicted by the Text
rules.explanation: Check each option against the passage.
rules.structure: A is false (he did not buy the bicycle); B is false (he never regretted); D is false (he walks to school).
notes: Only C is supported.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: He sacrificed his own plan to help a friend and did not regret it, so C is the best inference.
rules.structure: Passage evidence → Option C.
notes: Correct answer: C.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing A because a bicycle is mentioned in the passage.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose C, which reflects his actions and attitude.
common_mistakes.reason: The bicycle is mentioned as a plan he did not carry out.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing B because he now walks to school.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose C, because the passage says he has never regretted his decision.
common_mistakes.reason: Walking to school is a consequence, not a regret.

questions.passage: Last month, SMA Harapan opened a new reading corner in its library. The corner provides more than 500 new books, including novels, comics and science magazines. Students can borrow up to three books at a time for two weeks. The school plans to add computers and free Wi-Fi next year so that students can access digital resources. According to the librarian, visits to the library have increased by 40 percent since the reading corner opened.
questions.question: Which TWO statements are true according to the passage?

options.A: Students may borrow three books for two weeks.
options.B: The reading corner already has computers and free Wi-Fi.
options.C: Library visits have increased by 40 percent.
options.D: The library only provides science magazines.
options.E: The school will close the library next year.

details_explanation.explanation: The passage says students can borrow up to three books for two weeks (A) and that visits increased by 40 percent (C). Computers and Wi-Fi are planned for next year, not available now; the library has novels, comics and magazines; and the school is adding facilities, not closing the library.
details_explanation.introduction: This is a multiple-answer reading question. Each option must be checked individually against the passage.

rules.title: 1. Check Each Option Separately
rules.explanation: Do not stop at the first true option. Read all five options and verify each one.
notes: The question asks for TWO statements.

rules.title: 2. Watch for Tense and Time Markers
rules.explanation: Option B is a distractor because computers and Wi-Fi are planned for next year, not present now.
rules.structure: plans to add ... next year ≠ already has
notes: Small words like 'next year' change the truth value of an option.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: 'Up to three books ... for two weeks' matches A, and 'increased by 40 percent' matches C.
rules.structure: Correct answers: A and C.
notes: Option D is false because the corner provides novels, comics and science magazines.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing B because computers and Wi-Fi are mentioned.
common_mistakes.correct: Do not choose B; they will be added next year.
common_mistakes.reason: The passage describes a future plan, not a current facility.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing only one answer.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose both A and C.
common_mistakes.reason: The question explicitly asks for TWO true statements.

questions.passage: The traditional market in our town has undergone a remarkable transformation. Once crowded and poorly organized, it is now a clean and well-managed place. The local government, however, insists that the changes are not merely cosmetic; they reflect a deeper commitment to improving the livelihoods of small traders.
questions.question: The word 'cosmetic' in the passage is closest in meaning to ___

details_explanation.explanation: In this context, 'cosmetic' means 'only on the surface' or 'superficial', because the government says the changes are more than appearance only.
details_explanation.introduction: Vocabulary-in-context questions test the meaning of a word as it is used in the passage, not its most common dictionary meaning. The contrast with 'a deeper commitment' signals that 'cosmetic' means superficial.

rules.title: 1. Use the Surrounding Words
rules.explanation: Look at the contrast markers near the word. Here 'not merely cosmetic; ... a deeper commitment' shows a contrast between surface and depth.
rules.structure: not merely cosmetic = not only for appearance
notes: Contrast words like 'however' and 'deeper' guide the meaning.

rules.title: 2. Beware the Literal Meaning
rules.explanation: 'Cosmetic' literally relates to beauty products, but that meaning does not fit here.
rules.structure: Context meaning > dictionary meaning
notes: Option A is the trap answer.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: 'Superficial' matches the contrast with 'a deeper commitment'. 'Expensive' and 'permanent' do not fit the contrast at all.
rules.structure: cosmetic ≈ superficial → Option B.
notes: Correct answer: B — superficial.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing A because 'cosmetic' usually refers to beauty products.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose B because the context contrasts surface appearance with real depth.
common_mistakes.reason: The question asks for the meaning in this passage, not the most common meaning.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing D because the changes are described positively.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose B; the sentence says the changes are NOT merely cosmetic.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Permanent' is not supported by the contrast in the sentence.

questions.passage: Research has consistently shown that sleep plays a crucial role in learning. During deep sleep, the brain consolidates information gathered during the day, transferring it from short-term to long-term memory. Students who sacrifice sleep to study longer often perform worse than those who keep a regular sleep schedule. In short, a good night's sleep is not a luxury but a necessary part of effective study.
questions.question: What is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Students should study longer at night.
options.B: Sleep is essential for effective learning and memory.
options.C: Deep sleep is not important for teenagers.
options.D: Good students never stay up late.

details_explanation.explanation: The whole passage explains that sleep helps the brain consolidate information and that cutting sleep harms study results. The main idea is that sleep is essential for effective learning and memory.
details_explanation.introduction: A main-idea question asks for the overall point of the passage, not a single detail. The final sentence often summarises the main idea.

rules.title: 1. Look for the Topic Sentence and Conclusion
rules.explanation: The first and last sentences often state the main idea.
rules.structure: First sentence: sleep is crucial in learning. Last sentence: sleep is a necessary part of effective study.
notes: Both point to the same main idea.

rules.title: 2. Reject Details and Distortions
rules.explanation: Options that mention only one detail or that contradict the passage are wrong.
rules.structure: A and C contradict the passage; D is an extreme statement not made in the text.
notes: Be careful with absolute words like 'never' and 'always'.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Option B summarises the entire passage: sleep supports learning and memory.
rules.structure: Main idea → Option B.
notes: Correct answer: B.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing a true detail such as 'deep sleep consolidates information' as the main idea.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose the statement that covers the whole passage.
common_mistakes.reason: A main idea must be broad enough to include the whole text.

common_mistakes.wrong: Choosing an extreme statement like 'Good students never stay up late.'
common_mistakes.correct: Choose B, which reflects the passage without exaggeration.
common_mistakes.reason: The passage does not use absolute language.

questions.passage: When the company first allowed employees to work from home three days a week, many managers feared a drop in productivity. Six months later, however, the data told a different story: output had risen by twelve percent, and sick leave had fallen sharply. Employees reported feeling more focused, largely because they no longer faced two hours of commuting each day. Still, some managers argue that remote work weakens team spirit, and the company has responded by organising monthly face-to-face meetings.
questions.question: Which TWO statements are supported by the passage?

options.A: Productivity fell after the policy was introduced.
options.C: Before the policy, employees spent two hours commuting each day.
options.E: The company stopped holding face-to-face meetings.

details_explanation.explanation: The passage states output rose by twelve percent (B) and that employees no longer faced two hours of commuting each day, which means they did commute two hours before the policy (C).
details_explanation.introduction: This question asks which statements the passage supports. Each option must be checked against the text, including the logical implication in option C.

rules.title: 1. Verify Direct Statements
rules.explanation: Option B is stated directly: 'output had risen by twelve percent'.
rules.structure: output had risen by twelve percent → B ✓
notes: Direct statements are the easiest to confirm.

rules.title: 2. Verify Logical Implications
rules.explanation: Option C is not worded identically, but 'no longer faced two hours of commuting' logically means they used to commute two hours.
rules.structure: no longer + two hours of commuting → previously two hours
notes: Implications must be certain, not merely possible.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: A is false (output rose, not fell), D is false (sick leave fell), and E is false (monthly face-to-face meetings are organised).
rules.structure: Correct answers: B and C.
notes: Only B and C are supported by the passage.

common_mistakes.correct: Choose B; the fear did not become reality.
common_mistakes.reason: The fear is reported, but the data showed the opposite.

common_mistakes.wrong: Ignoring C because it is not worded exactly like the passage.
common_mistakes.correct: Choose C; 'no longer commute two hours' implies they did before.
common_mistakes.reason: Some correct options are paraphrased or implied.

questions.question: Click the incorrect part and type the correct form.
questions.sentence: My sister don't like spicy food.

name.id: Simple Present Negatif — Orang Ketiga Tunggal

details_explanation.explanation: 'My sister' is third-person singular, so the negative auxiliary must be 'doesn't' and the main verb stays in the base form: 'doesn't like'.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative simple present sentences use do/does + not + base verb. The auxiliary agrees with the subject; the main verb never takes -s.

rules.title: 1. Choose the Right Auxiliary
rules.explanation: Use 'don't' with I/you/we/they and plural subjects. Use 'doesn't' with he/she/it and singular subjects.
rules.structure: Singular third person + doesn't + base verb.
notes: 'My sister' = 'she', so 'doesn't' is needed.

rules.title: 2. Base Verb after the Auxiliary
rules.explanation: After do/does/don't/doesn't, always use the base verb, never the -s form.
rules.structure: doesn't + like (not 'likes')
notes: The -s ending is carried by the auxiliary 'does'.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The segment 'don't like' must become 'doesn't like' or 'does not like'.
rules.structure: My sister doesn't like spicy food.
notes: Correct answers: 'doesn't like', 'does not like'.

common_mistakes.correct: My sister doesn't like spicy food.
common_mistakes.reason: A singular subject requires 'doesn't'.

common_mistakes.reason: After 'doesn't', use the base verb.

details_explanation.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb: 'The news ... is very shocking'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns ending in -s are actually singular and uncountable: news, mathematics, physics, economics. They take singular verbs.

rules.title: 1. Singular Uncountable Nouns Ending in -s
rules.explanation: Words like news, mathematics, and physics look plural but are treated as singular.
rules.structure: The news is ... / Mathematics is ...
notes: The prepositional phrase 'about the earthquake' does not change the subject.

rules.title: 2. Ignore Prepositional Phrases
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with a noun inside a prepositional phrase.
rules.structure: The news (about the earthquake) + is
notes: 'Earthquake' is singular but it is not the subject.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The subject is 'The news', so 'are' must be changed to 'is'.
rules.structure: The news about the earthquake is very shocking to everyone.
notes: Correct answer: is.

common_mistakes.reason: Academic subjects ending in -s take a singular verb.

details_explanation.explanation: The present perfect uses have/has + past participle. The past participle of 'go' is 'gone', not 'went'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Go' has two different forms in the past: 'went' (simple past) and 'gone' (past participle). Only the past participle can follow have/has.

rules.title: 1. Present Perfect Form
rules.explanation: Use have/has + past participle for actions with a present result or indefinite past time.
rules.structure: She has gone / They have gone
notes: 'Went' is used only in the simple past: She went yesterday.

rules.title: 2. Irregular Past Participles
rules.explanation: Many common verbs have different simple past and past participle forms.
rules.structure: go–went–gone / do–did–done / see–saw–seen / write–wrote–written
notes: Check a verb list if you are unsure.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The segment 'has went' must become 'has gone'.
rules.structure: She has gone to the market to buy some vegetables.
notes: Correct answer: has gone.

common_mistakes.correct: She has gone to the market.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Went' is the simple past, not the past participle.

name.id: Kesesuaian Subjek-Kata Kerja dengan Klausa Relatif

details_explanation.explanation: The main subject is 'The report' (singular). The relative clause 'which was written by the manager' only describes it, so the main verb must be singular: 'was submitted'.
details_explanation.introduction: In a sentence with a relative clause, the main verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not with the noun inside the relative clause.

rules.title: 1. Find the Head Noun
rules.explanation: Remove the relative clause and check the remaining subject.
rules.structure: The report (which was written by the manager) + main verb
notes: The head noun is 'The report' — singular.

rules.title: 2. Do Not Agree with the Nearest Noun
rules.explanation: The noun closest to the verb ('the manager') is not the subject.
rules.structure: The report ... was submitted (not 'were')
notes: This is a common trap in academic writing.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The segment 'were submitted' must become 'was submitted'. 'Had been submitted' is also acceptable if the sentence refers to an earlier past event.
rules.structure: The report which was written by the manager was submitted late.
notes: Correct answers: 'was submitted', 'had been submitted'.

details_explanation.introduction: Students often confuse the preposition 'to' with the infinitive 'to'. After the preposition 'to' in expressions like 'look forward to', 'be used to', and 'object to', we use the -ing form.

rules.title: 1. Prepositional 'to' vs Infinitive 'to'
rules.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.
rules.structure: look forward to + noun/V-ing
notes: I look forward to the holiday. / I look forward to meeting you.

rules.title: 2. Other Fixed Expressions
rules.explanation: The same rule applies to 'be used to', 'object to', 'in addition to', and 'devote oneself to'.

rules.title: 1. Short Adjectives: -er

details_explanation.introduction: In the inverted third conditional, the auxiliary 'had' comes before the subject, and the main verb must be the past participle.

rules.title: 1. Inversion Structure
rules.explanation: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle.
rules.structure: Had I known..., I would have raised...
notes: The auxiliary 'had' carries the tense; the main verb is a participle.

rules.title: 2. Know–Knew–Known
rules.explanation: 'Knew' is the simple past; 'known' is the past participle used after 'had'.
rules.structure: I knew (past) / I had known (past perfect)
notes: The same pattern applies to see–saw–seen, go–went–gone.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: The segment 'knew' must become 'known'.
rules.structure: Had I known the answer, I would have raised my hand immediately.
notes: Correct answer: known.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I knew the answer, I would have raised my hand.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known the answer, I would have raised my hand.
common_mistakes.reason: After 'had', use the past participle.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I had knew the answer, I would have raised my hand.
common_mistakes.correct: If I had known the answer, I would have raised my hand.
common_mistakes.reason: The past perfect is 'had + past participle'.

details_explanation.explanation: 'The students' is plural, so the passive verb must be plural: 'were given', not 'was given'.
details_explanation.introduction: In the passive voice, the verb 'be' agrees with the subject. A plural subject requires 'were' in the past simple passive.

rules.title: 1. Passive Agreement
rules.explanation: The form of 'be' agrees with the subject of the passive sentence.
rules.structure: The student was given... / The students were given...
notes: Only one word changes: was → were.

rules.title: 2. Singular vs Plural Subjects
rules.explanation: Check whether the subject is singular or plural before choosing was/were.
rules.structure: was + singular / were + plural
notes: 'The students' is plural.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Change 'was given' to 'were given'. The other segments are correct.
rules.structure: The students were given a lot of homework by the teacher yesterday.
notes: Correct answer segment: 'was given' → 'were given'.

common_mistakes.wrong: The students was given a lot of homework.
common_mistakes.correct: The students were given a lot of homework.
common_mistakes.reason: A plural subject needs 'were'.

common_mistakes.correct: The student was given a lot of homework.
common_mistakes.reason: A singular subject needs 'was'.

details_explanation.explanation: The third conditional needs the past perfect in the if-clause ('had studied') and 'would have + past participle' in the result clause ('would have passed').
details_explanation.introduction: The third conditional describes an unreal situation in the past and its imagined result. Both clauses refer to the past, so neither 'would have' in the if-clause nor 'will' in the result clause is correct.

rules.title: 1. If-Clause Uses the Past Perfect
rules.explanation: Never use 'would have' in the if-clause.
rules.structure: If + subject + had + past participle
notes: Correct: If she had studied...
Incorrect: If she would have studied...

rules.title: 2. Result Clause Uses 'would have'
rules.explanation: The result of an unreal past condition is 'would have + past participle'.
rules.structure: subject + would have + past participle
notes: Correct: she would have passed.
'She will pass' is a real future, which does not match the past unreal meaning.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Two errors: 'would have studied' → 'had studied', and 'she will pass' → 'she would have passed'.
rules.structure: If she had studied harder last semester, she would have passed the final exam.
notes: Correct answers: 'had studied' and 'she would have passed'.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she would have studied harder, she would have passed.
common_mistakes.correct: If she had studied harder, she would have passed.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Would have' cannot appear in the if-clause.

common_mistakes.wrong: If she had studied harder, she will pass.
common_mistakes.correct: If she had studied harder, she would have passed.
common_mistakes.reason: An unreal past result needs 'would have + past participle'.

details_explanation.explanation: Two errors: 'which' refers to a person, so it must be 'who' or 'that'; and 'a lots of' is incorrect — use 'a lot of' or 'lots of'.
details_explanation.introduction: Relative pronouns depend on the noun they describe: 'who/that' for people, 'which/that' for things. Quantifiers also have fixed forms: 'a lot of' or 'lots of', never 'a lots of'.

rules.title: 1. Relative Pronouns for People
rules.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' when the antecedent is a person.
rules.structure: The teacher who/that teaches us...
notes: 'Which' cannot describe a person.

rules.title: 2. Quantifier Forms
rules.explanation: 'A lot of' and 'lots of' are correct; 'a lots of' does not exist.
rules.structure: a lot of + noun / lots of + noun
notes: Both are used with countable and uncountable nouns.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Change 'which' to 'who' or 'that', and 'a lots of' to 'a lot of' or 'lots of'.
rules.structure: The teacher who teaches us English always gives us a lot of homework.
notes: Correct answers: 'who'/'that' and 'a lot of'/'lots of'.

common_mistakes.wrong: The teacher which teaches us English is kind.
common_mistakes.correct: The teacher who teaches us English is kind.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Which' is for things, not people.

common_mistakes.wrong: She has a lots of friends.
common_mistakes.correct: She has a lot of friends.
common_mistakes.reason: 'A lots of' is never correct.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Despite' is used alone; 'in spite of' is the other correct form. 'Despite of' does not exist in standard English.
details_explanation.introduction: Both 'despite' and 'in spite of' mean 'although', and both are followed by a noun phrase or a gerund. They cannot be mixed into 'despite of'.

rules.title: 1. Correct Forms
rules.explanation: Use either 'despite + noun' or 'in spite of + noun'.
rules.structure: Despite the rain... / In spite of the rain...
notes: 'Despite of' is never correct.

rules.title: 2. Followed by a Gerund
rules.explanation: When a verb follows, use the -ing form.
rules.structure: Despite being tired, she kept working.
notes: Do not use 'although' with a noun phrase: 'Although the rain...' is incorrect.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Only 'Despite of' is wrong. Replace it with 'Despite' or 'In spite of'. The rest of the sentence is correct.
rules.structure: Despite the heavy rain, the football match was continued by the referee.
notes: Correct answers: 'Despite', 'In spite of'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Despite of the rain, the match continued.
common_mistakes.correct: Despite the rain, the match continued.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Despite' does not take 'of'.

common_mistakes.wrong: In spite the rain, the match continued.
common_mistakes.correct: In spite of the rain, the match continued.
common_mistakes.reason: 'In spite' requires 'of'.

name.en: Inversion with 'Not only' and Relative Pronouns
name.id: Inversi dengan 'Not only' dan Kata Ganti Relatif

details_explanation.explanation: Two errors: after 'Not only' the subject and auxiliary must be inverted ('Not only was he'), and 'what' cannot be used as a relative pronoun here — use 'that' or 'which'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Not only' at the beginning of a clause triggers inversion. Separately, relative clauses about things use 'that' or 'which', never 'what'.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after 'Not only'
rules.explanation: Move the auxiliary before the subject.
rules.structure: Not only + auxiliary + subject + main verb
notes: Not only was he late, but he also forgot...

rules.title: 2. Relative Pronouns for Things
rules.explanation: 'That' and 'which' introduce relative clauses about things. 'What' means 'the thing that' and cannot follow a noun.
rules.structure: the documents that/which were required
notes: 'The documents what were required' is incorrect.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Change 'Not only he was' to 'Not only was he', and 'what were required' to 'that were required' or 'which were required'.
rules.structure: Not only was he late, but he also forgot to bring the documents that were required.
notes: Correct answers: 'Not only was he' and 'that/which were required'.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not only he was late, but he also forgot the documents.
common_mistakes.correct: Not only was he late, but he also forgot the documents.
common_mistakes.reason: Fronted 'Not only' requires inversion.

common_mistakes.wrong: The documents what were required are missing.
common_mistakes.correct: The documents that were required are missing.
common_mistakes.reason: 'What' cannot act as a relative pronoun after a noun.

details_explanation.explanation: Two errors: 'suggest' is followed by a gerund ('suggested applying'), and 'decide' is followed by a full infinitive ('decided to follow').
details_explanation.introduction: Different verbs take different patterns. 'Suggest' takes a gerund (or 'that + clause'), while 'decide' takes 'to + base verb'. Using the wrong pattern produces errors like 'suggested me to apply' and 'decided to following'.

rules.title: 1. 'Suggest' + Gerund
rules.explanation: 'Suggest' is never followed by an object + infinitive.
rules.structure: suggest + V-ing / suggest + that + subject + verb
notes: Correct: He suggested applying for the scholarship.
Incorrect: He suggested me to apply.

rules.title: 2. 'Decide' + Full Infinitive
rules.explanation: 'Decide' takes 'to + base verb'.
rules.structure: decide + to + base verb
notes: Correct: I decided to follow his advice.
Incorrect: I decided to following.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Change 'me to apply' to 'applying' and 'to following' to 'to follow'.
rules.structure: He suggested applying for the scholarship, and I decided to follow his advice.
notes: Correct answers: 'applying' and 'to follow'.

common_mistakes.wrong: He suggested me to apply for the scholarship.
common_mistakes.correct: He suggested applying for the scholarship.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Suggest' takes a gerund, not an object + infinitive.

common_mistakes.wrong: I decided to following his advice.
common_mistakes.correct: I decided to follow his advice.
common_mistakes.reason: After the infinitive marker 'to', use the base verb.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Each of + plural noun' is grammatically singular, so the verb must be 'has to submit', not 'have to submit'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Each' focuses on individuals one by one, so it is singular even when it is followed by a plural noun phrase.

rules.title: 1. 'Each of' is Singular
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with 'each', not with the plural noun after 'of'.
rules.structure: Each of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: Each of the students has a locker.

rules.title: 2. Compare with 'All of'
rules.explanation: 'All of' takes a plural verb; 'each of' does not.
rules.structure: All of the students have lockers. / Each of the students has a locker.
notes: Notice the different verb forms.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: 'Have to submit' must become 'has to submit'. The pronoun 'their' is acceptable here as a neutral reference and is not an error.
rules.structure: Each of the students in my class has to submit their assignment before the deadline.
notes: Correct answer: 'has to submit'.

common_mistakes.correct: Each of the students has to submit the form.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Each of' is singular.

common_mistakes.wrong: Each of the student has to submit the form.
common_mistakes.correct: Each of the students has to submit the form.
common_mistakes.reason: 'Each of' must be followed by a plural noun.

details_explanation.explanation: 'No sooner' at the beginning of a sentence requires inversion: 'No sooner had I arrived ... than ...'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'No sooner ... than' is a fixed structure meaning 'immediately after'. When it begins the sentence, the subject and auxiliary are inverted.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after 'No sooner'
rules.explanation: Place the auxiliary 'had' before the subject.
rules.structure: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + clause
notes: No sooner had I arrived than the train left.

rules.title: 2. 'than', not 'when'
rules.explanation: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than'. 'Hardly/Scarcely ... when' is a different structure.
rules.structure: No sooner ... than / Hardly ... when
notes: The sentence already uses 'than' correctly.

rules.title: 3. Applying the Rule to This Question
rules.explanation: Change 'I had arrived' to 'had I arrived'. All other segments are correct.
rules.structure: No sooner had I arrived at the station than the train left.
notes: Correct answer: 'had I arrived'.

common_mistakes.wrong: No sooner I had arrived than the train left.
common_mistakes.correct: No sooner had I arrived than the train left.
common_mistakes.reason: 'No sooner' at the start requires inversion.

common_mistakes.wrong: No sooner had I arrived when the train left.
common_mistakes.correct: No sooner had I arrived than the train left.
common_mistakes.reason: 'No sooner' is followed by 'than', not 'when'.
